summary: Defines Attribute-Value Pairs that let Diameter natively carry cryptographic keying material, which some AAA applications need. It gives a standard way to deliver keys within Diameter messages. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes a guard must hand a secret key to someone. This memo says what labeled envelopes to use in Diameter for passing the key along.

questions: what is the diameter key avp
how are keys sent in diameter
subtitle: A standard Diameter container for carrying several cryptographic keys in one message.

tldr.problem: Diameter's EAP application allows at most one master session key AVP per message, but newer EAP key derivation and re-authentication work produces other keys that may also need to be sent between Diameter nodes.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6734 defines a grouped Key AVP (code 581) that holds a key type, the keying material and optionally a lifetime, a name and an SPI, so one message can carry several keys.
tldr.outcome: Keys that are not already protected must only travel over mutually authenticated TLS or IPsec. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Unprotected keys
facts.value: Mutually authenticated TLS or IPsec only

today: RFC 6734 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2012, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the Key AVP and its Key-Type registry.

sections.title: Why Diameter Needs Key AVPs
sections.content:
Some Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) applications must carry cryptographic keying material. The Diameter EAP application (RFC 4072) already defines the EAP-Master-Session-Key and EAP-Key-Name AVPs for keys produced by certain EAP methods. At most one instance of either of these may appear in any Diameter message.

Newer work, such as RFC 5295, derives further keys from the material created during an EAP exchange, and the EAP Re-authentication Protocol (RFC 6696) adds more keys that may need to move between Diameter nodes. RFC 6734 therefore specifies a set of AVPs that carry multiple keys in a single Diameter message.
sections.plainLanguage: The old envelope held just one key. Now there are more keys to send, so this memo makes a new envelope that can be used several times in one letter.

sections.title: Key Terms Used by the Specification
sections.content:
The RFC uses the RFC 2119 requirement words (MUST, SHOULD and so on) and defines four abbreviations for the key kinds it carries.

  • DSRK: Domain-Specific Root Key (RFC 5295).
  • MSK: Master Session Key (RFC 3748).
  • rMSK: re-authentication MSK, a per-authenticator key derived from the rRK.
  • rRK: re-authentication Root Key, derived from the Extended Master Session Key (EMSK) or from a DSRK.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the names of different kinds of keys, a bit like a master key, a building key and a room key that are all made from one another.

sections.title: The Grouped Key AVP
sections.content:
The Key AVP (AVP Code 581) is of type Grouped. It bundles the key type and the keying material and, optionally, a lifetime, a name for the key and a Security Parameter Index (SPI).

In the RFC's notation, Key-Type is required to appear (written with angle brackets), Keying-Material is required (curly braces), and Key-Lifetime, Key-Name and Key-SPI are optional (square brackets). Any other AVPs may follow. Because the Key AVP is a container, a message can hold several of them, one per key.
sections.plainLanguage: The Key AVP is a box with slots. One slot must say what sort of key it is, one must hold the key, and the other slots are extras like a label and an expiry date.

sections.title: The Five Inner AVPs
sections.content:
Each part of the Key AVP has its own AVP.

  • Key-Type (582, Enumerated) names the kind of key: DSRK (0), rRK (1) or rMSK (2). New values are assigned by IANA under the Specification Required policy.
  • Keying-Material (583, OctetString) holds the key itself. How it is used depends on the key type and the link layer, and is outside the scope of the document.
  • Key-Lifetime (584, Unsigned32) is the number of seconds the keying material is valid.
  • Key-SPI (585, Unsigned32) holds an SPI value that can be used with other parameters to identify associated keying material.
  • Key-Name (586, OctetString) is an opaque key identifier. How it is generated depends on the key type and usage, and is also out of scope.

Applications SHOULD treat the lifetime as starting when the message carrying the key is received. Clients SHOULD check that the value is reasonable; for example, a key should not generally live longer than the session lifetime.
sections.plainLanguage: Each slot in the box has a name and a code number. The key slot holds the secret, the lifetime slot says how many seconds it works, and the name slot is a label so people can tell keys apart.

sections.title: Protecting Keys in Transit
sections.content:
The RFC calls transporting keys a security-sensitive action. Some keying material is already protected and can safely cross the open Internet. If a Key AVP contains a Keying-Material AVP that is not already protected, the Diameter messages carrying it MUST only be sent protected by mutually authenticated TLS or IPsec.

The security considerations of the Diameter base protocol (RFC 6733) apply, as do those in Section 8.4 of RFC 4072.
sections.plainLanguage: If a secret key is not already locked in a box, it has to travel in an armored truck, and both ends must prove who they are before the truck is loaded.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA assigned AVP codes 581 to 586 under the policy in RFC 6733: Key (581), Key-Type (582), Keying-Material (583), Key-Lifetime (584), Key-SPI (585) and Key-Name (586).

IANA also created a registry of Key-Type values and filled it with the three values above. New values use the Specification Required policy (RFC 5226), and once a value is assigned it MUST NOT be deleted, replaced or modified.
sections.plainLanguage: A librarian wrote down the official code numbers for each slot, and promised that once a key type gets a number, that number never changes meaning.
